posts.text:
The barreleye fish has a see-through head.

Its two tube-shaped eyes sit inside a clear, fluid-filled dome. For 50 years scientists thought they were stuck staring straight up.

In 2008 a camera caught them swiveling forward.
comments: Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute solved it with a live fish on video. The dome may be armor: the barreleye picks prey out of stinging siphonophore tentacles.

posts.text: What cheap toy has outlasted every expensive one for your pet?
comments: Cardboard box, bottle cap, or something stranger?

posts.text:
How a clownfish lives in a sea anemone without getting stung:

Anemones fire when they sense sugars called sialic acids. A 2025 study found clownfish keep normal levels everywhere except their skin mucus, where they turn them down.

The anemone's own mucus has almost none.
comments: The researchers' phrase for it was Trojan horse: the fish may be borrowing the trick the anemone uses to avoid stinging itself.

posts.text: Did you know? A bull moose grows a whole new set of antlers every year. They take three to five months to grow, can reach five feet across and weigh up to 77 pounds, then drop off after the rut.
Fun Fact: A walrus climbs out of the sea with its teeth. To get onto an ice floe it jams its tusks into the ice and hauls its whole body up.

The basilisk lizard runs on water.

Fringes of skin on its long back toes unfurl to add surface area, and each foot slaps straight down, trapping a pocket of air that holds it up.

About 15 feet at 5 feet a second, then it sinks and swims.
comments: Central Americans call it the Jesus Christ lizard. It only runs on its hind legs; the front ones tuck up out of the way.

posts.text: Post the best photo you've ever taken of your pet.
comments: Blurry ones with a story attached count.

posts.text:
Baby discus fish eat their parents.

Not all of them. Both parents ooze a skin mucus the fry bite off and feed on, for up to a month.

A 2010 study found the mucus spikes with antibodies right as the fry start swimming, much like a mammal's first milk.
comments: There is even a weaning period, about three weeks after the fry go free-swimming, when the parents start shaking them off.

posts.text: Did you know? A tapir's nose is a short trunk that doubles as a snorkel. On land it grabs branches and strips off the leaves. In the water the tapir can stay under for several minutes with just the tip poking up.

Fun Fact: A porcupine carries about 30,000 quills, each tipped with 700 to 800 microscopic barbs. Its skin also makes an antibiotic, which helps an animal that sometimes falls out of trees and quills itself.

Dung beetles navigate by the Milky Way, and the proof came from a planetarium.

Researchers in Johannesburg projected only the Milky Way, no individual stars. The beetles found their way out fast.

With only scattered bright stars and no Milky Way, they took much longer.
comments: Their eyes cannot resolve single stars. They see the galaxy as one fuzzy stripe across the sky and steer by that.

posts.text: How many nicknames does your pet have, and which one does it answer to?
comments: Bonus if the one it answers to is not the one on the vet record.

posts.text:
Green anacondas do not lay eggs.

Females give birth to live young, in the water, usually 20 to 40 at a time. The record litter was 82.

They breed only every other year. It takes that much out of them.
comments: Bigger mothers have bigger litters, and the females are much larger than the males to begin with.

posts.text: Did you know? The bump on a beluga whale's forehead, called the melon, changes shape on purpose. It is a lump of fat the whale can reshape, and scientists think that helps aim the sonar it uses to find food and breathing holes in the Arctic ice.

Fun Fact: The northern short-tailed shrew is a venomous mammal. Its saliva carries a toxin potent enough to subdue prey larger than the shrew itself, the strongest venom known among shrews and their relatives.

A hungry cat hides a baby's cry inside its purr.

The solicitation purr carries an unusually high frequency buried in the normal low rumble, in roughly the range of a human infant's cry.

People rate it as more urgent and less pleasant, even people who have never owned a cat.
comments: The cats in the study only produced it when asking for food. The ordinary resting purr does not carry the cry.

posts.text: What is your pet irrationally afraid of?
comments: Vacuum cleaners are the obvious one. We want the strange ones.

posts.text:
A cherry shrimp eats its own skin.

Like every arthropod, it grows by shedding its exoskeleton. Then it turns around and eats the cast-off shell to reabsorb the nutrients still locked inside.

Nothing wasted.
comments: Keepers who scoop the molts out of the tank are taking away a meal. Leave them in.

posts.text: Did you know? A beaver's front teeth never stop growing, and their enamel is reinforced with iron. Daily gnawing is what keeps them trimmed to a working length.
Fun Fact: A raccoon's front paws work better wet. In nerve recordings, wetting the skin made the touch fibers fire more readily and respond to lighter pressure.

Shave a tiger and it is still striped.

The pattern is in the skin, not just the fur. Vets who sedate a tiger and shave it for surgery say the skin looks tattooed.

Every tiger's stripes are unique, so camera traps count wild tigers the way a fingerprint identifies a person.
comments: Much of what we know about how many wild tigers are left comes from exactly that: remote cameras and stripe matching.

posts.text: Who or what is your pet's sworn enemy?
comments: The mail carrier is taken. Who else?

posts.text:
A honeybee swarm picks a new home without counting votes.

Scouts dance for rival sites. Once about 15 scouts land on one cavity at the same time, they signal the swarm to warm up for takeoff, even while others still dance for somewhere else.
comments: Cornell researchers watched the takeoff signal happen the moment the 15-bee quorum formed at the winning site.

posts.text: Did you know? The streaked tenrec of Madagascar makes sound with its quills. Muscles under the skin rub a patch of spines together, producing frequencies from about 2 to 80 kilohertz, most of it too high for human ears.

Fun Fact: The hellbender, North America's largest salamander, breathes almost entirely through its skin. The loose folds along its sides add surface area for pulling oxygen out of the water, and its lungs mostly handle buoyancy.

Male red-footed tortoises cluck like chickens.

It happens during courtship, and it sounds genuinely like a chicken, in a group of animals most people assume are silent.
comments: Zookeepers at San Francisco Zoo describe the clucking as part of the mating process. Tortoises are not silent, just quiet.

posts.text: What did you believe about your pet's species that turned out to be wrong?
comments: Ours: that a ball python skipping meals meant something was wrong. Usually it does not.

posts.text:
A sea otter has pockets.

A loose patch of skin under each forearm works as a pouch. On one dive it can stash several clams or urchins, then bring the whole haul to the surface and eat floating on its back.
comments: The pockets leave its paws free to keep hunting on the same dive. At the surface it uses its chest as the table.

posts.text: Did you know? Bull elk bugle in September and October, a loud, wailing call that marks the start of the mating season. You hear it most at dawn and dusk.

Fun Fact: A giant anteater has no teeth and a two-foot tongue anchored to its breastbone. It flicks that tongue up to 150 times a minute, coated in sticky saliva, and takes only about 140 insects from each mound before moving on.

A numbat can eat 20,000 termites in a day.

That is about a tenth of its body weight, gathered with a tongue that reaches at least 5 centimeters past its nose.

It is World Numbat Day, and there are only a few hundred of them left.
comments: Unlike almost every other marsupial, the numbat is active only by day. It keeps the same hours as the termites it eats.

posts.text: What has your bird learned to say that it should not have?
comments: And who taught it? Be honest.

posts.text:
A narwhal's tusk is a tooth, and it can feel.

It spirals up to nine feet out of one side of a male's head. Researchers mapped a sensory pathway from the tusk to the brain, and narwhals respond measurably when water of different saltiness washes over it.
comments: It grows through the upper lip, almost always on the left side. A tooth, not an antler and not a horn.

posts.text: Did you know? The colugo is the champion glider among mammals. It drops from the forest canopy, sails more than the length of two football fields, and can make 90-degree turns before landing gently on a trunk.
Fun Fact: A muskrat can chew underwater without swallowing a drop. Its lips close behind its front teeth, sealing the mouth, and it can stay down for as long as 20 minutes.
